---
title: "Tests on building instance trackers on object detection results"
author: "Botond Ortutay"
output: pdf_document
---

### Situtation overview

This document is a summary of tests run on the instance tracker built for the l3f browser app `src/main.js` -> `InsDetTracker`. We aim to see how well the current tracker is able to handle known problem situations such as

 - **size variance between detections** of same real-world object (attempted solution: using the calculated center points as the authoritative location data rather than the bbox info as outputted by the detector directly)
 - individual real-world object **may not be detected over every frame** while actually being in the image & **occasional ghost-detections** (detection registered by detector matching no actual real world object); (attempted solution: adding 'TENTATIVE' & 'TEMPORARILY_MISSING' statuses to tracked object & warmup & missing item logic)
 - **"flip-flopping" or "category flipping"**; when a real world object is detected as belonging to different object categories between each frame (attempted solution: keeping category history data for individual tracked objects & taking this into account when predicting future locations of objects)

And whether better solutions can be found during the analysis. Most obviously by optimizing the following config constants:

```javascript
/**
 * Constants governing tracking configuration.
 */
const TRACKER_CONFIG = {
  // Lifecycle thresholds
  CONFIRMATION_FRAMES: 2,     // Required consecutive detections before promotion from TENTATIVE
  MISSING_FRAMES_LIMIT: 5,    // Consecutive missed frames before marking DELETED

  // Matching thresholds (in pixel space)
  LOOSE_MATCH_DISTANCE_PX: 40,   // Standard match threshold for category matches/flip-flops
  TIGHT_MATCH_DISTANCE_PX: 15,   // Strict threshold for mismatched categories without flip-flop history
  BACKUP_MATCH_DISTANCE_PX: 60   // Velocity-direction alignment fallback threshold
};
```

This analysis is conducted on multiple measurements.

### Setup

#### Tests
  
Each of the tests are done with a sampling rate of 8fps and with a measurement duration of about one minute. The tracker config is the same for every measurement in measurement run 1.

```{r}
# Read one JSON object per line, preserving each record as a list.
read_jsonl <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  lapply(lines, jsonlite::fromJSON, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

print_track_timeline <- function(records) {
  # The first record is metadata; remaining records are frames.
  frames <- Filter(
    function(x) identical(x$record_type, "frame"),
    records
  )

  for (frame in frames) {
    timestamp <- frame$tracker_state$timestamp
    tracks <- frame$tracker_state$tracks

    if (length(tracks) == 0L) {
      cat(sprintf("[%s] Active tracks: none\n", timestamp))
      next
    }

    track_labels <- vapply(
      tracks,
      function(track) {
        instance_id <- track$instanceId %||% "?"
        category <- track$currentCategory %||% "unknown"
        status <- track$status %||% "unknown"

        sprintf("%s [%s]: %s", instance_id, category, status)
      },
      character(1)
    )

    cat(sprintf(
      "[%s] Active tracks: %s\n",
      timestamp,
      paste(track_labels, collapse = " | ")
    ))
  }
}

# Helper for providing a fallback when a field is NULL.
`%||%` <- function(x, y) {
  if (is.null(x)) y else x
}

# Function to split a string into N-character chunks
chunk_string <- function(s, width = 90) {
  n <- nchar(s)
  if (n <= width) return(s)
  starts <- seq(1, n, by = width)
  ends <- pmin(starts + width - 1, n)
  substring(s, starts, ends)
}



print_category_history_values <- function(data, data_name = deparse(substitute(data))) {
  # Keep only frame records
  frame_records <- Filter(
    function(record) identical(record$record_type, "frame"),
    data
  )

  # Collect categoryHistory from every track in every frame
  histories <- unlist(
    lapply(frame_records, function(record) {
      tracks <- record$tracker_state$tracks

      if (is.null(tracks) || length(tracks) == 0) {
        return(list())
      }

      lapply(tracks, function(track) {
        track$categoryHistory
      })
    }),
    recursive = FALSE
  )

  # Handle the case where no tracks or histories were found
  if (length(histories) == 0) {
    cat(
      "Here are all the different categoryHistory values in tracks ",
      "in frame-records in ", data_name, ":\n\n",
      "(No categoryHistory values found.)\n",
      sep = ""
    )
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }

  # Convert each history to a consistent JSON representation
  history_json <- vapply(histories, function(history) {
    if (is.null(history)) {
      return("null")
    }

    jsonlite::toJSON(
      history,
      auto_unbox = TRUE,
      null = "null",
      na = "null",
      pretty = FALSE
    ) |>
      as.character()
  }, character(1))

  # Print unique values, preserving their first-seen order
  unique_histories <- unique(history_json)

  cat(
    "Here are all the different categoryHistory values in tracks ",
    "in frame-records in ", data_name, ":\n\n",
    paste(unique_histories, collapse = "\n"),
    "\n",
    sep = ""
  )

  invisible(unique_histories)
}

# Function for producing (timestamp, hasBeenConfirmed-count) pairs over a tX
confirmed_tracks_over_time <- function(data) {
  keep <- which(vapply(
    data,
    function(record) identical(record$record_type, "frame"),
    logical(1)
  ))

  map_dfr(keep, function(i) {
    record <- data[[i]]
    tracks <- record$tracker_state$tracks

    confirmed_count <- if (is.null(tracks) || length(tracks) == 0) {
      0L
    } else {
      sum(vapply(
        tracks,
        function(track) isTRUE(track$hasBeenConfirmed),
        logical(1)
      ))
    }

    tibble(
      timestamp_ms = record$timestamp_ms,
      confirmed_tracks = confirmed_count
    )
  })
}

plot_track_trajectories <- function(records, width = 640, height = 480) {

  points <- map2_dfr(records, seq_along(records), function(record, i) {
    tracks <- record$tracker_state$tracks

    if (is.null(tracks) || length(tracks) == 0) {
      return(tibble())
    }

    map_dfr(tracks, function(track) {
      center <- track$center

      if (is.null(center) ||
          is.null(center$centerX) ||
          is.null(center$centerY)) {
        return(tibble())
      }

      tibble(
        frame = i,
        timestamp_ms = as.numeric(record$timestamp_ms),
        track_id = as.character(track$instanceId),
        x = as.numeric(center$centerX),
        y = as.numeric(center$centerY)
      )
    })
  })

  if (nrow(points) == 0) {
    stop("No track centers found in the supplied records.")
  }

  points <- points %>%
    distinct(track_id, x, y, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
    arrange(track_id, frame)

  # Create a segment from each center to the next center of that track.
  segments <- points %>%
    group_by(track_id) %>%
    mutate(
      xend = lead(x),
      yend = lead(y)
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(xend), !is.na(yend)) %>%
    ungroup()

  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(
      data = segments,
      aes(
        x = x, y = y,
        xend = xend, yend = yend,
        color = track_id
      ),
      arrow = grid::arrow(
        length = grid::unit(0.15, "inches"),
        type = "closed"
      ),
      linewidth = 0.8,
      lineend = "round"
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = points,
      aes(x = x, y = y, color = track_id),
      size = 2.5
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      position = "top",
      limits = c(0, width),
      breaks = seq(0, width, by = 80),
      expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
    scale_y_reverse(
      limits = c(height, 0),
      breaks = seq(0, height, by = 60),
      expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
    coord_fixed() +
    labs(
      title = "Track trajectories",
      x = "X coordinate (pixels)",
      y = "Y coordinate (pixels)",
      color = "Track ID"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "right"
    )
}
```

### Data exploration

#### On the dataformat in general
  
Tracking results are saved in the following format:

 - .jsonl
 - First line is per-measurement metadata
 - Rest of the lines are `(detection, state)`-pairs, where
   - `detection` is neural network output generated by feeding our model a frame sample from the webcam stream
   - `state` is the internal state representation generated by feeding `detection` to `InsDetTracker.updateState()` where the state has already consumed the previous history, so $State_n = State_{n-1}.updateState(detection, timestamp)$

To showcase this more clearly; Here are concrete examples of the contents of `t2`:  

First 5 lines:

```{r}
cat(paste(unlist(lapply(seq_along(head(readLines("tracking_2_multiple_objects_stationary.jsonl", warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"), 5)), function(i) {
  chunks <- chunk_string(head(readLines("tracking_2_multiple_objects_stationary.jsonl", warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"), 5)[i], width = 90)
  c(paste0("--- Line ", i, " ---"), chunks)
})), collapse = "\n"), "\n")
```

Last 10 lines:

```{r}
cat(paste(unlist(lapply(seq_along(tail(readLines("tracking_2_multiple_objects_stationary.jsonl", warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"), 10)), function(i) {
  chunks <- chunk_string(tail(readLines("tracking_2_multiple_objects_stationary.jsonl", warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"), 10)[i], width = 90)
  c(paste0("--- Line ", i, " ---"), chunks)
```

### Data exploration: qualitative analysis

Here's what merely examining the output data tells us:  

#### `categoryHistory` recording seemingly broken in the dataformat  
  
Looking at the first 5 lines and last 10 lines of the contents of `t2` we 
printed out: Specifically where `"record_type":"frame"`: for each track in 
`tracker_state.tracks` `categoryHistory` always seems to be `{}`. To confirm 
that the data is indeed broken we wrote the `print_category_history_values` 
to iterate over each measurement result and print out all unique category 
history values. We'll run it on all of our data now:

```{r}
print_category_history_values(t1)
print_category_history_values(t2)
print_category_history_values(t3)
print_category_history_values(t4)
print_category_history_values(t5)
print_category_history_values(t6)
print_category_history_values(t7)
```

This confirms that category history saving in our data is broken. This 
warrants further investigation.  

#### Rapid movement problematic for tracking  
  
This is clearly seen since we conduct measurements which differ from each 
other in movement speed and also performance. In `t1` we have a single 
stationary object. In `t3` we have a single slowly moving object and in `t4` 
we have a single repidly moving object. By looking at the timeline of the 
last 20 frames for each of these measurements we see:

```{r}
print_track_timeline(tail(t1, 20))
print_track_timeline(tail(t3, 20))
print_track_timeline(tail(t4, 20))
```

In `t1` only two objects are tracked over the experiment lifetime. In `t3` 16 
objects are tracked and in `t4` 52 objects are tracked. So by increasing 
movement speed of the tracked objects generated tracks seemingly increase 
which points in the direction of a worsening tracking quality on increasing 
speed.  
  
Since `t1`, `t3` and `t4` are all single-item experiments, the tracker works 
optimally when there is exactly one track in the state. Otherwise:

 - Less than one track means that the tracker doesn't track enough things (likely due to not receiving enough consecutive detections)
 - More than one track means that the tracker tracks too many things (likely due to ghost detections, location prediction failure causing track fragmentations or unsuccesful flip-flop protections causing track fragmentation)

Here we graphically represent the amount of tracks in the status we have 
confirmed over the three different measurents

```{r}
ggplot(confirmed_tracks_over_time(t1), aes(x = timestamp_ms,
                         y = confirmed_tracks)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Previously confirmed tracks over time: single stationary object (t1)",
    x = "Timestamps",
    y = "Previously confirmed tracks in state"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

So here as one can see tracking is *practically perfect*. At no time does the 
tracking break and at no point does the tracker track too many objects.

```{r}
ggplot(confirmed_tracks_over_time(t3), aes(x = timestamp_ms,
                         y = confirmed_tracks)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Previously confirmed tracks over time: single slow-moving object (t3)",
    x = "Timestamps",
    y = "Previously confirmed tracks in state"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Here we see:

 - A few instances of track loss
 - On instance of more than one simultaneous track (early on, before 430000)
 - The big track loss around 440000 is particularly large. Probably due to bad detections or environmental complications rather than mere motion-related track loss

```{r}
ggplot(confirmed_tracks_over_time(t4), aes(x = timestamp_ms,
                         y = confirmed_tracks)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Previously confirmed tracks over time: single rapid-moving object (t4)",
    x = "Timestamps",
    y = "Previously confirmed tracks in state"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Here we see:

 - Many instances of track loss. A lot more frequent than in `t3`. Likely due to increased speed. So speed increase would seem to correspond to track loss frequency
 - We four cases of double tracking. Likely caused by unsuccesful category-flip-guarding causing double tracking (these are also notably small durations, which supports this theory!!) These too seems to increase in frequency as speed grows.

  

I also want to highlight instances with **seemingly obvious instances of rapid speed breaking tracking**

 1. instance: measurement 4, timestamps 18433 to 19308 (inclusive)

```{r}
print_track_timeline(t4[92:99])
```

*#10* and *#11* are likely the same object:

 - both detected as bowls
 - there is only one real-life object we attempt to track in `t4`
 - here's how the timeline likely went:
   1. Tracker gets new location for object *#10* at $18682$. New velocity calculation made, new location predicition made.
   2. No detections at $18807$, therefore *#10* marked `TEMPORARILY_MISSING`
   3. New detection at $18931$, doesn't match `LOOSE_MATCH_DISTANCE_PX`, (possibly not even `BACKUP_MATCH_DISTANCE_PX`), therefore it is marked as a new track even though it matches the category of *#10*

Us not being able to match the new detection at $18931$ to the prediction 
produced at $18682$ is a consequence of the following things:

 - the missing frame at $18807$
   - which if we assume this movement happens at a large velocity itself points to the hypothesis that the tracker is less reliable when the speed increases (due to worse detections)
 - an inaccurate prediction
   - due to us not being able to update location & velocity estimations at $18807$
   - or maybe the matching distances are too tight for a high velocity
   - or maybe acceleration/slowdown makes the predictions themselves wrong.

But to see how true our hypothesis is by looking at the trajectories of these 
tracks:

```{r}
plot_track_trajectories(t4[92:99])
```

So here the hypothesis that only rapid speed broke the tracking can be 
discarded, since *#11* does not correspond to the direction *#10* was moving. 
Since *#11* is only detected for a single frame, this is likely a ghost.

 2. instance: measurement 4, timestamps 35443 to 36193 (inclusive)

```{r}
print_track_timeline(t4[228:234])
```

By the same logic as above (all items are bowls, only one real life item is 
being moved in front of the camera), we make the same assumption here too 
(*#23*, *#24* and *#25* are the same item, which is given three different 
`instanceID`s due to the real world item "outrunning" the tracker's 
loose/backup matching treshold). Once again let us draw the trajectories of 
the tracked items in this pre-specified timeframe:


```{r}
plot_track_trajectories(t4[228:234])
```

It is highly unlikely that all three tracks *#23*, *#24* and *#25* would be 
the same object, since this would require notable accelerations and direction 
changes in a few frames' timespan. However, notably *#25* roughly matches the 
direction *#23* was travelling towards so this may or may not be an actual 
case of a failed match (note: *#23* is still being tracked when *#25* appears) 
but at least *#24* is a ghost making these instances too not so obviously a 
case of tracking broken by rapid movement speed.
